title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
lede: An arXiv paper reports an open 27B model that inspects its own weights and graded answers, diagnoses a failure and edits the weights directly, improving without gradient updates.

points: The authors call the method self-rewriting: the model acts as its own optimizer using only forward passes.
Its edit raised accuracy by 6.6 points on held-out problems, and accuracy rose across eight consecutive editing sessions.
Edits are tested on practice problems and kept only if they help.
It restored a damaged copy of itself to over 80% of the original accuracy on unseen image tasks.
Within one model family only the largest model improved; smaller ones made no edit or broke themselves.

points.text: A top comment says the only fix the model found was shortening its reasoning traces to stay under the token limit.
Readers argue over the no-training claim: testing edits and keeping winners looks like optimization, though it avoids backprop.
Several think these weight-editing papers inspire more than they deliver, with models making simple scripted tweaks for now.
Safety worries recur: a self-editing model could in principle suppress the activations tied to alignment.
